message.content:
The sea doesn’t have a single, fixed color—it looks different depending on a few key factors:

| Factor | Effect on Color |
|--------|-----------------|
| **Depth** | Shallow water reflects the sky, so it can look light blue or even greenish. Deeper water absorbs longer wavelengths (reds, oranges) and scatters shorter wavelengths (blues, violets), giving a deeper blue or indigo hue. |
| **Clarity / Turbidity** | Clear water lets you see the seabed and any underlying colors (sand, coral, algae). Turbid or algae‑rich water can appear greenish or brownish. |
| **Sunlight / Angle** | The sun’s position changes the intensity and shade of blue. Early morning or late afternoon light can give a warmer, golden tint. |
| **Surface Conditions** | Calm water reflects the sky more directly, making it look bluer. Rough waves scatter light, often giving a more muted or even white‑washed appearance. |
| **Substrate & Life** | Underwater vegetation, coral, or sediment can tint the water green, orange, or even reddish. |

So, while we often think of the sea as “blue,” it can range from pale turquoise near the shore to deep indigo in the open ocean, with greenish or even brownish tones appearing under certain conditions.
